strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: the paper convincingly quantifies that visual feature extraction dominates inference time in existing joint encoders (83–93%), explaining why multimodal rerankers are absent in practice.

Sensible and practical design: caching vision tokens offline, compressing them with an attention-based adapter, and using a compact language model (MiniLM) yields a genuinely favorable accuracy–efficiency profile (33M joint-encoder parameters, ~2ms online inference vs ~100ms for BLIP-2).

Fair comparisons: prior joint encoders (ALBEF, BLIP, BLIP-2) are evaluated under the same cached-vision regime, and embedding baselines are reproduced via OpenCLIP with verified agreement with reported numbers.

Good empirical coverage: multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) at multiple scales/resolutions, plus ablations on token count, pool size, training objectives, and distillation, including results in the appendix.
Well written and clearly structured; the step-by-step design narrative (Sections 3.1–3.4) with key takeaways makes the contribution easy to follow.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the individual components are all established — precomputed/cached vision features (ColBERT/ColPali-style late interaction), learnable-query token compression (essentially a Q-Former, which the authors acknowledge), and an LLaVA-style projection into a small LM. The contribution is primarily an engineering combination rather than a new method.

Mismatch between claims and evaluation: despite the title and abstract emphasizing 'large scale' retrieval, all experiments are on 1,000-image Flickr30k test sets and COCO Karpathy splits with a reranking pool of k=10. There is no evaluation at actual retrieval scale (millions of candidates), no end-to-end latency measurements of the full two-stage pipeline, and no demonstration that the 50k pairs/sec throughput claim holds in a realistic system.

Storage advantage is overstated: 49kB/image for 1M images is ~49GB and grows linearly; the paper does not compare against compression alternatives (e.g., product quantization of raw tokens, token pruning/merging like ToMe, or simply caching a CLIP embedding), so the Pareto frontier of storage-vs-accuracy is not established.

Restricted benchmark scope: only two datasets, both image-caption retrieval; no multilingual, no out-of-domain, no error bars or statistical significance testing, and only R@1 highlighted in the main comparison table.

Some inconsistencies and loose ends: the ablation in Table 4 labels the third objective 'ITC' while Section 4 calls it 'text-embedding recovery'; a few results in Table 1 show regressions (e.g., CLIP ViT-B R@10 91.8→91.7) that go undiscussed; code and checkpoints are only promised 'shortly', limiting reproducibility at review time.

The token-compressed variant still trails the uncompressed local variant and BLIP-2 in accuracy (86.9 vs 88.6 Flickr R@1), so the practical win is mostly efficiency; a deeper analysis of when compression hurts (e.g., fine-grained/localized queries) would strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated practical problem: the vision-extraction bottleneck that has prevented joint-encoder rerankers from being used in large-scale multimodal retrieval, and Section 3.1 quantifies this bottleneck clearly.
The overall system design is sensible and clearly presented: offline precomputation of vision tokens, a compact language model for joint encoding, and a token-compression adapter to reduce storage.

The evaluation covers multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) and multiple resolutions, includes ablations on compression ratio, pool size, training objectives, and distillation, and reports useful efficiency metrics (storage, parameters, latency).

The two-phase training recipe (hard-negative mining, MLM, text-embedding recovery, local-to-compressed distillation) is described in enough detail, with hyperparameters in the appendix, to support reproducibility once code is released.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core components. The token-compression adapter is essentially a Q-Former/Perceiver resampler (the authors themselves note the connection to BLIP-2), caching vision tokens follows ColBERT/ColPali-style late interaction, and projecting vision tokens into a language model embedding space is the standard LLaVA recipe. The contribution is primarily an engineering combination of known techniques, with no new insight or analysis of why the combination works.

The 'large scale' claims are not backed by any large-scale experiment. All evaluations are on Flickr30k and COCO, small benchmarks with 1k–5k images. Despite framing around web-scale retrieval, there is no experiment over millions of candidates, no disk/indexing throughput measurement, and no demonstration that the 49kB/image storage claim is practical at scale (at 1B images this is ~49TB).

The efficiency comparison in Table 2 is somewhat unfair in EDJE's favor: ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 inference times assume cached vision features (their actual end-to-end latency would be much worse), while the storage cost that EDJE introduces to gain this advantage is reported but not factored into the headline '53× faster' claim of Figure 1b.

The central claim that EDJE 'matches prior art' is stronger than the evidence. In Table 2, BLIP-2 outperforms the local variant on both Flickr-ZS (88.6/96.9 vs 87.8/96.5) and COCO-FT (66.3/83.5 vs 64.9/81); 'matching' holds only for the ViT-B class of baselines. The compressed variants lose further accuracy.

Missing comparisons to obvious alternative efficiency baselines: token pruning/merging methods (e.g., ToMe), perceiver-style compression applied directly to existing joint encoders, or rerankers built on top of generative VLMs. The paper does not establish that its specific design is the best way to exploit cached vision features.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce confidence: the abstract claims 50k pairs/second while Table 2 implies ~33k (64 pairs / 1.91ms); Figure 4 and the ablations are described in the text but the objectives ablation is split between main text and appendix in a confusing way; minor typos ('To goal of this section', 'These states are than passed').

Only Recall@1 appears in the main comparison table, and with a reranking pool of k=10 the Recall@10 results in Table 1 are nearly identical to the base embedding model (e.g., 91.7 vs 91.8), which is expected but means the 'improvements' are confined to a narrow reordering of the top 10 — the practical impact on a real retrieval pipeline with much larger candidate pools is not demonstrated.
The paper positions itself as a 'proof of concept' (Section 6), which conflicts with the deployment-oriented claims of the abstract and further weakens the significance case for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly identifies the vision backbone as the dominant inference bottleneck (83–93% of runtime) in existing joint encoders, which explains why multimodal rerankers are absent from practical retrieval pipelines; the efficiency analysis in Section 3.1 is informative and quantified.

Simple but effective design: combining offline vision-token caching with a lightweight token-compression adapter and a small language model (MiniLM) yields a practical reranker with a strong accuracy–efficiency profile (33M parameters, ~2ms inference for batch of 64, 49kB/image storage) versus prior joint encoders (139–167M parameters, ~83–102ms).

Extensive empirical coverage: results span multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2), scales, and resolutions (Table 1); comparisons to ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 under a controlled cached-vision regime with matched training data (Table 2) make the comparison reasonably fair.

Useful ablation studies: token-count trade-off curves, pool-size robustness, training-objective ablations, and distillation ablations isolate the contribution of each design component; hyperparameters are reported in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

The two-phase training recipe (hard-negative mining, MLM, text-embedding recovery, local-to-compressed distillation) is well described and each component is ablated, showing measurable gains (e.g., +3.1 R@1 from distillation for the 64-token variant).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the token-compression adapter is essentially a Q-Former (BLIP-2) / Perceiver resampler, and offline caching of vision tokens is standard practice in VLM pipelines; the contribution is primarily an engineering recombination of known ideas rather than a new technique.

The central motivating claim of large-scale (web-scale) retrieval is never directly evaluated: experiments are limited to Flickr30k (1,000 test images) and COCO (Karpathy split), where reranking pools of size 10 are trivial to search; no experiments at even moderate scale (e.g., millions of candidates, end-to-end latency including retrieval, storage at real scale) substantiate the '50k pairs/second' and web-scale deployment claims.

Some headline numbers are not clearly supported: the 53× speedup and 50k pairs/sec throughput claims are not broken down or verified in the tables; Table 1 shows the reranker can hurt R@10 (e.g., CLIP ViT-B/16: 91.8 → 91.7), and improvements are concentrated on R@1, which should be discussed.

Minor inconsistency between the main text and appendix: Section 4 describes a 'text-embedding recovery' objective with a cosine loss, while the appendix ablation (Table 4) reports 'ITC' (text–image contrastive learning); these appear to be different objectives, creating ambiguity about what was actually trained.

Compressed variants are only compared on Flickr in detail; COCO results for compression trade-offs and the effect of the text-embedding recovery loss on compressed models are incomplete, and compressed variants slightly underperform the local variant on COCO without analysis of why.

Writing has several typos and loose phrasing ('To goal of this section', 'These states are than passed'), and Figure 1b conflates zero-shot Flickr performance with efficiency claims in a way that could be read as stronger than the evidence.
Scaling the approach is only partially explored: only one language model (MiniLM-L12) is tested, so the modularity claim is not empirically validated across language backbones.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the paper convincingly identifies visual feature extraction as the bottleneck preventing joint-encoder re-rankers from being used at scale (Section 3.1, Figure 1), and the proposed solution — offline vision precomputation plus a lightweight adapter and compact language model — is a sensible and practically relevant paradigm shift.

Strong empirical execution: comparisons against ALBEF, BLIP, and BLIP-2 across multiple axes (accuracy, storage, parameter count, latency) under a controlled cached-vision regime; consistent gains over multiple embedding backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) demonstrate modularity as a drop-in re-ranker.

Comprehensive ablations and analyses: token-count trade-off curves, pool-size robustness, training-objective ablations (ITM/MLM/ITC), local-to-compressed distillation, cross-model negative mining, token-compression baselines (striding, clustering, attention pruning), quantization (FP8/FP4), and I/O benchmarking of token fetching. This level of thoroughness is above average.

Practical relevance: the 53x inference speedup, 49kB/image storage, and throughput numbers are meaningful for real deployment; the pseudo-code and I/O analysis (Appendix C) show attention to systems-level concerns often ignored in academic papers.
Interpretability analysis (Section 5.4, Appendix D) providing qualitative and quantitative evidence that compressed tokens retain semantic content adds credibility to the compression claim.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components are largely assembled from existing ideas — attention-pooling/query-based token compression is essentially a Q-Former layer (which the authors acknowledge), offline caching of visual features is standard in cross-attention architectures and recalls LightningDOT, and the training recipe (ITM + MLM + distillation) closely mirrors BLIP. The contribution is a well-engineered system rather than a new method.

Evaluation is confined to small academic benchmarks (Flickr30k, COCO) with a re-ranking pool of k=10-100. Despite 'large-scale' claims in the title and abstract, there is no experiment at web scale (millions/billions of candidates), where storage (49kB/image => ~50TB per billion images even before quantization), index maintenance, and candidate-generation quality would be the real challenges.

The comparison regime in Table 2 assumes precomputed visual features for EDJE but appears to compare against joint encoders whose online cost includes vision encoding; the fairness of this asymmetric setup deserves more scrutiny, and prior joint encoders could also cache vision features if re-designed (the paper argues they cannot, but the comparison conflates architecture with deployment strategy).

The re-ranker is tied to the retriever's vision backbone (hard negatives must be mined with a well-aligned embedding model per Appendix E), which limits the 'modularity' claim — swapping retrievers requires re-training and re-indexing.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL in footnote 1 is empty in the manuscript; some experimental details (pre-training compute budget, number of steps/epochs, hardware for training) are missing; several minor writing issues ('To goal of this section', 'We than repeated', lowercase 'kokitsi Maninis') and a confusing double-row presentation in Table 1 reduce polish.

Zero-shot Flickr gains partly depend on the retriever: the DFN/MetaCLIP improvements are small and DFN is itself Flickr-filter-tuned, so the headline numbers partly reflect backbone choice rather than the re-ranker.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and well-motivated problem: the visual feature-extraction stage makes existing joint encoders (BLIP/BLIP-2) impractical as re-rankers, and quantifies this bottleneck clearly (Figure 1a, Section 3.1).

The core design — offline vision precomputation + lightweight token-compression adapter + a compact LM as the joint encoder — is sensible, modular, and well-articulated with a clear build-up across Sections 3.1–3.4.

The evaluation is broad for a systems-flavored paper: multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) and resolutions, ablations on token count, pool size, training objectives, distillation, negative-mining models (Appendix E), token-compression baselines (Appendix G), quantization (Appendix H), and I/O considerations (Appendix C.1).
The full-dataset retrieval protocol (Appendix F, LightningDOT setup) is a more realistic stress test than the standard 1k-image splits, and EDJE shows substantial gains there.
The interpretability analysis of compressed tokens (Sections 5.4, D) is a nice touch, suggesting most native ViT tokens are redundant for retrieval.
The efficiency claims are internally consistent: storage (49kB/image), parameter count (33M), and online latency (1.9–2.9ms vs 83–101ms for BLIP) are all reported and support the headline claims.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the combination of precomputed visual tokens (ColBERT/ColPali-style), a Q-Former-like learnable-query compression layer (BLIP-2), and a small cross-encoder re-ranker is a straightforward composition of well-known components. The paper acknowledges the connection to Q-Former and attention pooling but does not clearly delineate what is fundamentally new beyond the system integration.

Benchmark coverage is narrow and saturated: only Flickr30k (zero-shot) and COCO (fine-tuned) are used, where R@5/R@10 are near ceiling (97–99.9%). No evaluation on harder, larger-scale, or more modern retrieval benchmarks where differences would be meaningful (e.g., larger candidate pools beyond the LightningDOT protocol, domain-shifted data, or web-scale-style evaluation). The 'large scale' claim in the title is only demonstrated at the throughput level, not with retrieval quality at scale.

Baseline fairness concerns: (i) the comparison to BLIP/BLIP-2 in Table 2 counts only their online joint-encoding cost while assuming precomputed vision features, but BLIP's cross-attention architecture could also cache ViT outputs; a cached-feature BLIP baseline would isolate how much of the gain comes from compression vs. simply swapping in a smaller LM; (ii) BLIP-2 was trained on 400M pairs vs. EDJE's 12M, so 'matching prior art' conflates data-scale differences with architectural ones.

The headline 'matching prior art' is somewhat generous: Compressed-64 trails BLIP-2 on both Flickr-ZS (86.9 vs 88.6) and COCO-FT (64.6 vs 66.3), and the evaluation asymmetry (zero-shot Flickr vs fine-tuned COCO) makes cross-condition comparisons harder to interpret.

Retrieval improvements over strong modern embedding baselines are modest where it matters most: for MetaCLIP and DFN the gains are small, and for SigLIP2 the absolute R@1 delta (~2–5 points) comes on a benchmark where the baseline is already at 82–95, raising questions about practical significance for well-tuned production pipelines.

Several important details are deferred or underspecified in the main text: the training-objective and negative-mining ablations are relegated to appendices with only summaries, the fine-tuning/pre-training data splits and hyperparameters would need verification for reproducibility, and the claim of '50k image-text pairs/second' lacks a clear end-to-end accounting (including I/O, which Appendix C.1 suggests roughly doubles per-query cost at large pools).

The system's dependence on a matched embedding model for negative mining (Appendix E shows large degradation with a weaker miner) somewhat undermines the 'drop-in re-ranker for any pipeline' framing, since performance is coupled to the retriever's quality and geometry.

Writing and presentation issues: Table 1's paired-row format (baseline vs EDJE) is confusing without clearer labeling; typos ('To goal of this section', 'states are than passed'); and key comparative claims sometimes rely on figures with limited axis detail (Figure 10).

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper convincingly identifies the vision backbone as the bottleneck preventing joint-encoder re-rankers from being deployed at scale, and supports this with concrete timing measurements (Section 3.1, Figure 1).

The proposed design (offline vision precomputation + lightweight token-compression adapter + compact LM joint encoder) is sensible, modular, and well explained, with a clear taxonomy (Figure 2) and a step-by-step build-up of the design decisions.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) and resolutions, direct comparison to ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 on accuracy, storage, parameters, and latency (Table 2), and a difficult full-dataset retrieval protocol following LightningDOT where EDJE shows large gains (Tables 8-9).

Thorough ablations: training objectives (ITM/MLM/ITC), local-to-compressed distillation, pool-size sensitivity, token-compression baselines (striding, clustering, attention pruning), cross-model negative mining, quantization (FP8/FP4), and I/O cost analysis of token fetching — this level of analysis is above average.

Strong efficiency results: 49 kB per image, ~2 ms inference for a batch of 64, ~50k pairs/sec, with quantization further reducing storage; the I/O benchmarking in Appendix C.1 is a nice practical touch.
Interpretability analysis of compressed tokens (Appendix D) provides qualitative and quantitative evidence that compression preserves semantic alignment.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is essentially a combination of known components — VLM-style vision token projection (LLaVA), Q-Former/Perceiver-style query-based token compression (explicitly acknowledged by the authors), and standard cross-encoder re-ranking with ITM/MLM objectives from ALBEF/BLIP. The paper itself frames the contribution as a 'proof of concept', which weakens the case for a top-tier venue.

Evaluation scale is modest relative to the 'large scale' claim in the title: experiments are on Flickr30k and COCO with re-ranking pools of k=10 to 100; the 50k pairs/sec and billion-scale storage claims are never validated in an actual large-scale retrieval setting (e.g., millions of candidates, end-to-end latency at scale).

Comparison fairness concerns: in Table 2, baselines (BLIP/ALBEF/BLIP-2) are evaluated under an assumed 'cached-vision regime' that those models were never designed or trained for; the inference-time comparison isolates only the joint-encoding component of the baselines, which somewhat favors the framing of the 53x speedup. On COCO fine-tuned, EDJE (64.9/81.0) actually trails BLIP-2 (66.3/83.5), so 'surpasses or matches' is slightly overclaimed.

The re-ranker reuses the retriever's own vision backbone and embedding model for negative mining, so some of the reported gains over embedding models (e.g., the +15% Recall@1 over CLIP) partly reflect capacity and training differences rather than purely the value of joint re-ranking; the cross-model mining ablation (Appendix E) shows sensitivity to miner choice but the practical implications for heterogeneous pipelines remain underexplored.

Reproducibility gaps: the code URL is left blank in the manuscript; training compute (GPU hours), number of epochs/steps, and full distillation schedule are not reported, making reproduction of the 12M-pair pre-training non-trivial.
Some writing issues: typos ('To goal of this section', 'are than passed', 'an order of magnitude'), and Figure 4's pool-size text slightly mismatches the ablated token counts (256 vs 576 discussion).

Scope limitations acknowledged but not fully addressed: only English, image-only modality, MiniLM text encoder fixed in main experiments, and no evaluation on harder fine-grained or compositional retrieval benchmarks.
